questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a rule of law from a rule of morality?

readLink.label: Read: What law is, and why business needs it →

options.text: A rule of law is always written down, while a rule of morality is not
options.explanation: Writing is not the test — custom is unwritten yet legally enforceable, and many written codes of conduct carry no legal force.

options.text: A rule of law is backed by the enforcing power of the State
options.explanation: Enforceability by the State — decree, fine, attachment, imprisonment — is exactly what converts a norm into law.

options.text: A rule of law binds only businesses, while morality binds individuals
options.explanation: Law binds every person, natural or artificial; the class of persons bound has nothing to do with the distinction.

options.text: A rule of law can never coincide with a rule of morality
options.explanation: Most legal rules (do not cheat, do not steal) are moral as well; overlap is normal, and the distinction lies in enforceability.

questions.stem: A wholesaler in Surat ships goods on credit to a buyer he has never met in Nagpur. The feature of a legal system that most directly makes that transaction possible is:

readLink.label: Read: What law is, and why business needs it →

options.text: The moral obligation of the buyer to pay what he owes
options.explanation: A moral obligation is precisely what the seller cannot rely on with a stranger — it carries no sanction he can invoke.

options.text: The power of the State to levy tax on the transaction
options.explanation: Taxation is a consequence of trade, not a reason a stranger can be trusted with credit.

options.text: Certainty — the seller knows in advance what a court will enforce if he is not paid
options.explanation: Certainty plus enforceability is what allows trade to extend beyond people one already trusts.

options.text: The freedom of trade guaranteed by Article 19(1)(g)
options.explanation: That freedom protects the right to carry on business against State interference; it does nothing to make a private buyer pay.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a source of law in India?

readLink.label: Read: The sources of Indian law →

options.text: Judicial precedent
options.explanation: The law declared by the courts is a recognised source, and by Article 141 the Supreme Court's declaration binds every court in India.

options.text: Customs and usage
options.explanation: A custom that is ancient, uniform, certain, reasonable and not opposed to statute is enforced as law.

options.text: Subordinate legislation
options.explanation: Rules, regulations and notifications made under a parent Act are a source, subject to staying within the Act.

options.text: A resolution of a company's board of directors
options.explanation: A board resolution binds only that company internally; it is a private act, not a source of the general law.

questions.stem: A rule made under a section of an Act says one thing and the section itself says another. The correct position is:

readLink.label: Read: The sources of Indian law →

options.text: The section prevails, and the rule is void to the extent of the inconsistency
options.explanation: Delegated legislation draws its life from the parent Act; a rule inconsistent with the section is ultra vires and cannot stand.

options.text: The rule prevails, being the later and more detailed statement
options.explanation: Recency and detail are irrelevant — a delegate can never rise above the authority that empowered it.

options.text: Both operate, and the person concerned may choose either
options.explanation: This treats an inconsistency as an option; the law resolves the conflict, it does not leave it to the citizen.

options.text: The conflict can be resolved only by Parliament amending the Act
options.explanation: A court can strike the rule down as ultra vires at once; no amendment is needed.

questions.stem: Parliament amends a section after the Supreme Court has interpreted it, so as to displace that interpretation. This shows that:

readLink.label: Read: The sources of Indian law →

options.text: A precedent is not a source of law at all
options.explanation: Precedent is a recognised source; the amendment changes the text being interpreted, it does not deny the source.

options.text: The amendment is invalid, since Article 141 makes the Court's declaration binding
options.explanation: Article 141 binds courts, not Parliament; the legislature is free to change the law prospectively.

options.text: A judgment interprets a statute rather than overriding it, so the legislature can alter the text that was interpreted
options.explanation: Precedent sits alongside the hierarchy — it explains what a provision means; changing the provision changes what there is to interpret.

options.text: The Supreme Court must now follow the earlier judgment in preference to the amended section
options.explanation: This inverts the relationship: courts apply the statute as it stands, and an interpretation of the old text does not survive its repeal.

questions.stem: An Act of Parliament is found to violate a Fundamental Right in Part III of the Constitution. Under Article 13 the Act is:

readLink.label: Read: The Constitution — the source above the sources →

options.text: Valid until Parliament itself repeals it, courts having no power over a duly passed Act
options.explanation: This denies judicial review; the Constitution is supreme precisely because a court may test an Act against it.

options.text: Void to the extent of the inconsistency with the Fundamental Right
options.explanation: Article 13 voids the offending law only so far as it is inconsistent; the rest of the Act can survive.

options.text: Void in its entirety, however small the offending part
options.explanation: This ignores the words 'to the extent of the contravention' — the whole Act falls only if the bad part is inseparable.

options.text: Voidable at the option of the person whose right is affected
options.explanation: Unconstitutionality is not a private option like a voidable contract; the law is void to that extent for everyone.

questions.stem: A High Court is asked to strike down a State Act on the ground that the policy behind it is economically unsound. The Court should:

readLink.label: Read: The Constitution — the source above the sources →

options.text: Strike it down, since judicial review extends to the wisdom of legislation
options.explanation: Judicial review tests legality, not wisdom; treating the two as the same is the commonest error on this topic.

options.text: Strike it down only if a majority of the Bench agrees the policy is unsound
options.explanation: The size of the majority cannot supply a ground of review that does not exist.

options.text: Refer the question to Parliament for an opinion
options.explanation: There is no such reference; the advisory route under Article 143 runs from the President to the Supreme Court, not from a court to the legislature.

options.text: Refuse relief, because a statute falls only for want of legislative competence or breach of a constitutional provision
options.explanation: Those two are the grounds of review; the merits of the policy are for the legislature.

questions.stem: A State law requires a licence to carry on the business of a commission agent in agricultural produce. A trader challenges it under Article 19(1)(g). The law is:

readLink.label: Read: The Constitution — the source above the sources →

options.text: Valid if the licensing requirement is a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public
options.explanation: The freedom of trade is not absolute; reasonable restrictions in the public interest are expressly permitted, which is why licensing regimes stand.

options.text: Void, because Article 19(1)(g) guarantees an absolute freedom to carry on any business
options.explanation: No Article 19 freedom is absolute — each is read with its own restriction clause.

options.text: Void, because trade and commerce is a Union List subject
options.explanation: Trade and commerce *within a State* is a State List entry; the competence objection does not arise on these facts.

options.text: Valid only if Parliament ratifies the State law
options.explanation: No ratification is needed for a State law on a State subject; ratification ideas belong to the repugnancy rule on Concurrent subjects.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Bill to Act · Money Bill
questions.stem: A Money Bill may be introduced:

readLink.label: Read: Legislation — how a Bill becomes an Act →

options.text: In either House of Parliament, like any other Bill
options.explanation: That is the rule for an ordinary Bill; a Money Bill is the express exception to it.

options.text: Only in the Rajya Sabha
options.explanation: This reverses the rule — the Rajya Sabha may only recommend changes to a Money Bill, it cannot originate one.

options.text: Only in the Lok Sabha
options.explanation: Money Bills originate in the popular House alone; the Council of States has a limited recommendatory role thereafter.

options.text: In a joint sitting of both Houses
options.explanation: A joint sitting is a device to resolve deadlock on an ordinary Bill; it is not a place of introduction, and it is unavailable for Money Bills.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Bill to Act · Assent and commencement
questions.stem: A Bill passed by both Houses receives the President's assent on 12 August 2026. Section 1(3) says the Act shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may by notification appoint. No notification has been issued. On 1 October 2026 the Act:

readLink.label: Read: Legislation — how a Bill becomes an Act →

options.text: Is in force, since an Act operates from the date of the President's assent
options.explanation: Assent converts the Bill into an Act; it does not bring the Act into operation where the Act itself defers commencement to a notification.

options.text: Is in force, since more than thirty days have passed since assent
options.explanation: There is no thirty-day default; the commencement clause governs, and it points to a notification.

options.text: Has lapsed for want of notification within sixty days
options.explanation: This borrows the lapse idea from Ordinances; an Act does not lapse if commencement is delayed.

options.text: Is on the statute book as an Act but is not yet in force
options.explanation: Assent and publication make it an Act; commencement waits for the notification, and different sections may be notified on different dates.

questions.stem: An Ordinance promulgated by the President under Article 123:

readLink.label: Read: Legislation — how a Bill becomes an Act →

options.text: Has the same force as an Act of Parliament, but ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved earlier
options.explanation: That is the bargain: full legislative force while it lasts, coupled with a short life and a requirement of legislative approval.

options.text: Has only the force of subordinate legislation
options.explanation: This confuses an Ordinance with rules made under an Act; an Ordinance is primary legislation in substance.

options.text: May be promulgated at any time, including while both Houses are in session
options.explanation: The power arises only when Parliament (or the House concerned) is not in session and immediate action is necessary.

options.text: Continues indefinitely until expressly repealed by Parliament
options.explanation: This drops the automatic expiry that distinguishes an Ordinance from an Act.

questions.stem: At which stage of a Bill's passage through a House does clause-by-clause consideration and amendment take place?

readLink.label: Read: Legislation — how a Bill becomes an Act →

options.text: The first reading
options.explanation: The first reading is introduction and publication only; the merits are not debated then.

options.text: The second reading
options.explanation: The second reading carries the general discussion, any committee reference, and the clause-by-clause consideration with amendments.

options.text: The third reading
options.explanation: By the third reading the text is settled; the Bill is voted on as a whole and only formal changes are possible.

options.text: After the President's assent
options.explanation: Once assent is given there is an Act, and it can be altered only by an amending Act.

questions.stem: A new subject arises that appears in none of the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule. Power to legislate on it lies with:

readLink.label: Read: Who may make which law — the three Lists →

options.text: The State Legislatures, the Union having only enumerated powers
options.explanation: That is the United States position; the Indian Constitution places the residue with Parliament.

options.text: Both, concurrently, until Parliament occupies the field
options.explanation: A subject does not become Concurrent merely because it is unlisted; the residue is assigned outright.

options.text: Nobody, until the Constitution is amended to add the subject to a List
options.explanation: No amendment is needed — Article 248 exists precisely so that no subject is left without a legislature.

options.text: Parliament, under the residuary power in Article 248
options.explanation: Residuary legislative power, including the power to impose a tax not mentioned in the Lists, vests in Parliament.

questions.stem: A Union law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject are irreconcilably in conflict. The State law did not receive the President's assent. The position is:

readLink.label: Read: Who may make which law — the three Lists →

options.text: The State law prevails within the State, being the more local law
options.explanation: Locality is not the test; Article 254 gives primacy to the Union law on Concurrent subjects.

options.text: Both laws are void, and the field is left unregulated
options.explanation: Repugnancy does not destroy the Union law; only the State law yields, and only to the extent of the conflict.

options.text: The Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of the repugnancy
options.explanation: That is Article 254(1) — with the exception, not applicable here, of a State law reserved for and receiving the President's assent.

options.text: The later of the two laws prevails, whichever legislature made it
options.explanation: A 'later in time' rule applies between laws of the same legislature; it does not govern a Union–State repugnancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs a subject with the correct List?

readLink.label: Read: Who may make which law — the three Lists →

options.text: Banking — Union List; bankruptcy and insolvency — Concurrent List
options.explanation: Banking is a Union subject, while bankruptcy and insolvency sits in the Concurrent List, which is why Parliament and the States have both legislated in that area.

options.text: Banking — State List; contracts — Union List
options.explanation: Both halves are inverted: banking is Union, and contracts are Concurrent.

options.text: Agriculture — Concurrent List; stock exchanges — State List
options.explanation: Agriculture is a State subject and stock exchanges are a Union subject; this swaps them into the wrong Lists.

options.text: Trade and commerce within a State — Union List; insurance — Concurrent List
options.explanation: Intra-State trade is a State subject and insurance is a Union subject, so both entries are misplaced.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Delegated legislation · Identifying the instrument
questions.stem: The Companies (Incorporation) Rules 2014 are best described as:
questions.sourceRef: Rules made under s. 469, Companies Act 2013

readLink.label: Read: Delegated legislation →

options.text: Primary legislation, having been laid before Parliament
options.explanation: Laying is a control mechanism over delegated legislation; it does not turn rules into an Act.

options.text: Subordinate legislation made by the Central Government under a rule-making power in the Act
options.explanation: Rules are made by the Government under an express empowering section and have the force of law so long as they stay within it.

options.text: Regulations made by a statutory regulator under its own Act
options.explanation: That describes SEBI or RBI regulations; these Rules are made by the Government under the Companies Act.

options.text: An administrative circular with no force of law
options.explanation: A circular is administrative and cannot create rights or liabilities; rules made under a statutory power can.

questions.stem: A section empowers the Government to make rules 'prescribing the form of the annual return'. A rule made under it also imposes a penalty of ₹10,000 for late filing. The rule is:
questions.sourceRef: Doctrine of ultra vires in delegated legislation

readLink.label: Read: Delegated legislation →

options.text: Valid in full, since rules have the force of law once notified
options.explanation: Notification gives a rule effect only if the rule was within power in the first place; it cannot cure an excess of authority.

options.text: Valid, because a penalty is necessary to make the form requirement effective
options.explanation: Necessity is not a source of power; a penal liability must be traceable to the Act itself.

options.text: Ultra vires and void so far as it imposes the penalty, the empowering words extending only to prescribing the form
options.explanation: A delegate can do only what the parent section authorises; the form-prescribing part stands, the penal part does not.

options.text: Valid until Parliament annuls it when it is laid before the House
options.explanation: Laying is one control, but a court can strike an ultra vires rule down without waiting for Parliament to act.

questions.stem: A department issues a general circular stating that a statutory exemption available under a section 'shall not apply to companies with turnover above ₹50 crore'. The section contains no such limit. The circular:

readLink.label: Read: Delegated legislation →

options.text: Is binding on the public, circulars being issued in the Official Gazette
options.explanation: Gazette publication belongs to notifications and rules; and even publication cannot make an administrative instruction override a section.

options.text: Is binding, because the department administers the Act and knows its intent
options.explanation: Administrative understanding is not a source of law; the words of the section govern.

options.text: Is binding only on companies below the ₹50 crore threshold
options.explanation: This invents a partial operation; the vice is that the circular cuts down a statutory exemption at all.

options.text: Cannot cut down the exemption given by the section, a circular being administrative and unable to create or take away a right
options.explanation: A circular guides officers and the public, but it cannot contradict the statute or withdraw a benefit the section confers.

questions.stem: A decision of the Supreme Court of India on the interpretation of a section of the Companies Act 2013 is binding on:

readLink.label: Read: Judicial precedent — stare decisis →

options.text: All courts and tribunals within the territory of India
options.explanation: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within the territory of India, tribunals included.

options.text: Only the High Court from which the appeal came
options.explanation: This confuses the binding force of a precedent with the parties and court in the particular appeal.

options.text: All courts, and also on Parliament, which cannot legislate contrary to it
options.explanation: Article 141 binds courts, not the legislature; Parliament may amend the provision that was interpreted.

options.text: All courts except tribunals, which are not courts
options.explanation: Tribunals exercising judicial functions are equally bound; their non-court label does not free them from Article 141.

questions.stem: In a judgment on a partnership dispute, a judge observes in passing that the same reasoning 'would apply equally to a limited liability partnership'. That observation is:

readLink.label: Read: Judicial precedent — stare decisis →

options.text: Part of the ratio decidendi, since it appears in the judgment
options.explanation: Appearing in the judgment is not the test — the ratio is the principle the decision actually rests on.

options.text: Obiter dictum — persuasive but not binding, the case not having concerned an LLP
options.explanation: It was not necessary to the decision on the facts, so it carries weight without binding force.

options.text: Binding on all lower courts if the judgment is of the Supreme Court
options.explanation: Article 141 binds courts to the law declared, which means the ratio; a passing remark does not acquire binding force from the level of the court.

options.text: Of no legal value whatsoever
options.explanation: This goes too far the other way — obiter of a superior court is persuasive and is regularly relied on in argument.

questions.stem: A district court in Karnataka is shown a judgment of the Bombay High Court on the very point in issue, and there is no decision of the Karnataka High Court or of the Supreme Court. The district court:

readLink.label: Read: Judicial precedent — stare decisis →

options.text: Is bound by it, a High Court being superior to a district court
options.explanation: Superiority alone is not enough — a High Court binds only the courts within its own territorial jurisdiction.

options.text: Must refer the matter to the Karnataka High Court before deciding
options.explanation: There is no such compulsory reference; the court decides and the losing party may appeal.

options.text: May treat it as persuasive but is not bound by it
options.explanation: A High Court's decision binds courts under it; in another State it carries persuasive value only.

options.text: Must ignore it entirely, judgments of other States being irrelevant
options.explanation: Not binding is not the same as irrelevant — courts routinely follow well-reasoned decisions of other High Courts.

questions.stem: The difference between overruling and reversal is that:

readLink.label: Read: Judicial precedent — stare decisis →

options.text: Overruling sets aside the principle laid down in an earlier, different case, while reversal alters the decision in the very same case on appeal
options.explanation: Overruling operates on the precedent; reversal operates on the case before the appellate court.

options.text: Overruling can be done only by the legislature, reversal only by a court
options.explanation: The legislature does not overrule; it amends the law. Both overruling and reversal are judicial acts.

options.text: Overruling applies to civil cases and reversal to criminal cases
options.explanation: Neither concept is confined to one stream of litigation.

options.text: Overruling and reversal are two names for the same thing
options.explanation: They are routinely confused, which is why the distinction is asked — one kills a precedent, the other flips a decision.

questions.stem: Which of the following would prevent a long-standing local practice from being recognised as a valid custom?

readLink.label: Read: Customs, usage and personal law →

options.text: That it is observed in one district only
options.explanation: A custom may be entirely local — locality is what most customs are about, not an objection to them.

options.text: That it has never been reduced to writing
options.explanation: Customs are by nature unwritten; the absence of a text is not a disqualification.

options.text: That it benefits traders more than consumers
options.explanation: A one-sided commercial effect is not itself a bar; unreasonableness in the legal sense means far more than an unequal advantage.

options.text: That it is opposed to a statutory provision
options.explanation: A custom must not conflict with a statute or public policy; where the statute covers the field, the statute prevails.

questions.stem: Personal law, as a source of Indian law, principally governs:

readLink.label: Read: Customs, usage and personal law →

options.text: The internal management of registered companies
options.explanation: That is company law, applicable to every company irrespective of the religion of its members.

options.text: Matters such as marriage, succession, adoption and maintenance, varying by community
options.explanation: Personal law is family and succession law applied according to the community of the parties; Paper 2 asks only that you recognise it as a source.

options.text: Commercial contracts between parties of the same community
options.explanation: Commercial contracts are governed by the Contract Act regardless of community; personal law has no role there.

options.text: The procedure to be followed in criminal trials
options.explanation: Criminal procedure is uniform and is now governed by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023.

questions.stem: The statement that India has an 'integrated judiciary' means that:

readLink.label: Read: The structure of the Indian judiciary →

options.text: A single hierarchy of courts, headed by the Supreme Court, enforces both Union and State laws
options.explanation: Unlike systems with parallel federal and state courts, one pyramid here handles laws made by either legislature, civil and criminal alike.

options.text: Every court in India has the same jurisdiction
options.explanation: Integration is about a single hierarchy, not identical powers — courts differ in subject-matter, territorial and pecuniary competence.

options.text: Union laws are tried by central courts and State laws by State courts
options.explanation: That describes the dual system India deliberately did not adopt.

options.text: Civil and criminal matters are heard by the same judge in every district
options.explanation: The district judiciary has distinct civil and criminal sides; integration refers to the single hierarchy, not to merged courtrooms.

questions.stem: Comparing the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 with that of a High Court under Article 226:

readLink.label: Read: The structure of the Indian judiciary →

options.text: Article 32 is wider, since the Supreme Court is the higher court
options.explanation: The rank of the court does not decide the width of the power; Article 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights.

options.text: The two are identical in scope, differing only in the court approached
options.explanation: This misses the words 'and for any other purpose' that appear in Article 226 and not in Article 32.

options.text: Article 226 is available only where Article 32 has first been tried
options.explanation: There is no such sequence; a party may move the High Court directly, and usually should.

options.text: Article 226 is wider in subject-matter, running for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose', while Article 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights
options.explanation: The High Court's power extends to enforcement of other legal rights as well, though it is limited territorially.

questions.stem: A litigant who has lost before a tribunal and has no statutory right of appeal seeks to move the Supreme Court. The provision he would invoke is:

readLink.label: Read: The structure of the Indian judiciary →

options.text: Article 131, the original jurisdiction
options.explanation: Article 131 covers disputes between the Union and States or between States, not a private litigant's appeal.

options.text: Article 143, the advisory jurisdiction
options.explanation: Article 143 is a reference by the President for the Court's opinion; a litigant cannot invoke it.

options.text: Article 136, special leave to appeal, which is discretionary and not a matter of right
options.explanation: Article 136 permits an appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal in India (other than a court martial), but only if the Court grants leave.

options.text: Article 227, superintendence over tribunals
options.explanation: Superintendence under Article 227 is a power of the High Court, not of the Supreme Court.

questions.stem: An order of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal is challenged on a question of law. The appeal lies to:

readLink.label: Read: The structure of the Indian judiciary →

options.text: The High Court having jurisdiction over the registered office of the company
options.explanation: This routes a company-law appeal the way an ordinary civil appeal would go; the Companies Act sends it straight to the Supreme Court.

options.text: The Supreme Court of India
options.explanation: An appeal from an NCLAT order lies to the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of that order.

options.text: The Central Government, NCLAT being a body under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
options.explanation: An appellate tribunal's judicial order is not reviewed by the executive that constituted it.

options.text: A larger Bench of the NCLAT itself
options.explanation: There is no such internal appeal; a larger-Bench mechanism belongs to the reconsideration of precedent, not to appeals from a tribunal.

questions.stem: A decree is passed by a civil court in a matter that a statute had exclusively assigned to a tribunal, both parties having consented to the civil court hearing it. The decree is:

readLink.label: Read: Jurisdiction — three questions before you file →

options.text: A nullity, since consent cannot confer subject-matter jurisdiction on a court that lacks it
options.explanation: Want of subject-matter jurisdiction goes to the root; such a decree can be questioned even at the stage of execution.

options.text: Valid, the parties having waived the objection by consenting
options.explanation: Waiver can cure some procedural objections but never supplies a competence the statute withheld.

options.text: Valid unless set aside in appeal within the limitation period
options.explanation: This treats a nullity as a merely erroneous decree; a nullity needs no appeal to be resisted.

options.text: Valid to the extent of the money claim but void as to any other relief
options.explanation: The defect is in the court's competence over the subject-matter, so it is not cured for part of the relief.

questions.stem: In a certain State, a Civil Judge (Junior Division) may try suits valued up to ₹15,00,000; above that and up to ₹2,00,00,000 the Senior Civil Judge is competent; beyond ₹2,00,00,000 the District Judge. A trader sues to recover the price of goods sold, ₹15,00,000, together with interest of ₹1,80,000 claimed as part of the sum due. The suit is to be filed before:
questions.sourceRef: Pecuniary jurisdiction — valuation of the suit

readLink.label: Read: Jurisdiction — three questions before you file →

options.text: The Civil Judge (Junior Division), the principal sum being exactly ₹15,00,000
options.explanation: This values the suit at the principal alone; the interest claimed as part of the sum due goes into the valuation and pushes it past the ₹15,00,000 ceiling.

options.text: The Civil Judge (Junior Division), interest never being counted for jurisdiction
options.explanation: Interest claimed as part of the amount sued for is part of the claim; treating it as always excluded is the trap in this question.

options.text: The District Judge, since a commercial claim must go to the highest civil court in the district
options.explanation: There is no such rule; a claim goes to the lowest court competent by value, and ₹16,80,000 is well below the District Judge's floor of ₹2,00,00,000.

options.text: The Senior Civil Judge, the suit being valued at ₹16,80,000
options.explanation: ₹15,00,000 + ₹1,80,000 = ₹16,80,000, which exceeds the Junior Division's ₹15,00,000 limit and is within the Senior Civil Judge's ₹2,00,00,000 limit.

questions.stem: Territorial jurisdiction in an ordinary civil suit is determined by:
questions.sourceRef: Territorial jurisdiction — residence, business, cause of action

readLink.label: Read: Jurisdiction — three questions before you file →

options.text: The residence of the plaintiff alone
options.explanation: Convenience of the plaintiff is not the test; the ordinary rule looks to the defendant and to the cause of action.

options.text: Where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action wholly or in part arose
options.explanation: These are the ordinary limbs, which is why a supplier may often sue either at the buyer's place or where delivery or payment was to be made.

options.text: The value of the claim
options.explanation: Value decides pecuniary jurisdiction, which is a different question from place.

options.text: The nature of the statute under which the claim arises
options.explanation: That bears on subject-matter jurisdiction, not on which district's court is competent.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Civil vs criminal · Standard of proof
questions.stem: A plaintiff sues for the price of goods delivered, and separately the same facts are the subject of a criminal complaint for cheating. The standards of proof are:
questions.sourceRef: Standard of proof in civil and criminal proceedings

readLink.label: Read: Civil proceedings and criminal proceedings →

options.text: Beyond reasonable doubt in both, the facts being identical
options.explanation: Identical facts do not merge the standards; each proceeding keeps its own, which is why one can succeed while the other fails.

options.text: Preponderance of probabilities in both, since a money claim underlies each
options.explanation: The presence of money does not soften the criminal standard; liberty is at stake in the complaint.

options.text: Preponderance of probabilities in the suit; beyond reasonable doubt in the criminal complaint
options.explanation: The civil plaintiff need only tilt the balance; the prosecution must exclude reasonable doubt, the accused being presumed innocent.

options.text: Beyond reasonable doubt in the suit; preponderance of probabilities in the complaint
options.explanation: This swaps the two standards — the single commonest error on this comparison.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Civil vs criminal · Parties and remedies
questions.stem: Which set correctly matches a civil proceeding?

readLink.label: Read: Civil proceedings and criminal proceedings →

options.text: Plaintiff and defendant · plaint · decree for damages or injunction
options.explanation: Those are the civil labels throughout — parties, initiating document and outcome all line up.

options.text: Prosecution and accused · complaint · conviction or acquittal
options.explanation: Every element here belongs to a criminal proceeding.

options.text: Plaintiff and accused · complaint · decree for damages
options.explanation: This mixes the two vocabularies — a plaintiff faces a defendant, not an accused, and a suit begins with a plaint.

options.text: Prosecution and defendant · plaint · sentence of imprisonment
options.explanation: Another mixture: a prosecution proceeds against an accused, and a plaint never leads to a sentence.

questions.stem: The essential feature that distinguishes arbitration from mediation and conciliation is that:
questions.sourceRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996; Mediation Act 2023

readLink.label: Read: Alternative dispute resolution →

options.text: Arbitration is conducted in private, while mediation and conciliation are public
options.explanation: All three are private; privacy is what they share, not what separates them.

options.text: Only arbitration requires a written agreement between the parties
options.explanation: Parties may agree in writing to mediate or conciliate as well; the form of the agreement is not the dividing line.

options.text: Only arbitration is available after a suit has been filed
options.explanation: The opposite is nearer the truth — a court may refer a pending suit to any of these methods.

options.text: In arbitration the tribunal decides the dispute and its award binds the parties, whereas a mediator or conciliator only assists them to settle
options.explanation: Arbitration is adjudicatory; mediation and conciliation leave the decision with the parties, a conciliator being able at most to propose terms.

questions.stem: Which statement is CORRECT as the law stands on 28 February 2026?
questions.sourceRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 Part III; Mediation Act 2023

readLink.label: Read: Alternative dispute resolution →

options.text: A conciliator may not make any proposal for settlement, his role being purely facilitative
options.explanation: That describes a mediator; a conciliator may formulate and reformulate terms of a possible settlement.

options.text: A mediated settlement agreement is merely a contract, enforceable only by a fresh suit
options.explanation: Under the Mediation Act 2023 such an agreement is final and binding and is enforceable as if it were a judgment or decree of a court.

options.text: A settlement agreement signed at the end of a conciliation has the same status and effect as an arbitral award
options.explanation: That is the effect the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 gives it, which is why it can be enforced without a fresh suit.

options.text: An award of a Lok Adalat may be appealed against to the District Court
options.explanation: A Lok Adalat award rests on consent; it is deemed a decree of a civil court and no appeal lies against it.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · ADR · Setting aside an award
questions.stem: A party dissatisfied with an arbitral award applies to court asking it to re-appreciate the evidence and decide the dispute afresh. The court will:

readLink.label: Read: Alternative dispute resolution →

options.text: Re-hear the matter fully, an award being only a recommendation
options.explanation: An award is binding, not a recommendation, and enforcement follows in the same manner as a decree.

options.text: Decline to sit in appeal on the merits, an award being open to challenge only on the limited statutory grounds
options.explanation: Section 34 lists narrow grounds; the whole point of arbitration would be lost if a court could redecide the dispute.

options.text: Refer the dispute to a fresh arbitral tribunal as of right
options.explanation: There is no automatic re-arbitration on a party's dissatisfaction.

options.text: Set the award aside because a party is dissatisfied with it
options.explanation: Dissatisfaction is not a ground; if it were, every losing party would have a remedy on demand.

questions.stem: A sub-section is followed by the words 'Provided that …'. That part of the section:

readLink.label: Read: How to read a bare Act →

options.text: Carves an exception out of the provision to which it is attached, and is read strictly
options.explanation: A proviso qualifies the provision it follows; because it is an exception, words like 'only' or 'exclusively' in it are read narrowly.

options.text: Extends the meaning of a word used in the section
options.explanation: Extending or clarifying meaning is the work of an Explanation, not of a proviso.

options.text: Applies to every section of the Act
options.explanation: A proviso operates on the provision it is attached to, not across the whole statute.

options.text: Illustrates how the provision is to be applied to particular facts
options.explanation: That is what an Illustration does, and an illustration can never control the section's language.

questions.stem: An illustration appended to a section appears to cover the assessee's facts, but the words of the section, read plainly, do not. The correct approach is:

readLink.label: Read: How to read a bare Act →

options.text: The illustration prevails, being the legislature's own application of the section
options.explanation: This treats an illustration as binding text; it is an aid to understanding and cannot enlarge the section.

options.text: The illustration prevails if it is more recent than the section
options.explanation: Illustrations are enacted with the section and carry no independent date or force.

options.text: Neither applies, and the matter falls outside the Act altogether
options.explanation: The section still governs the field; a mismatch with an illustration does not remove the subject from the statute.

options.text: The section prevails; an illustration helps in understanding but cannot control or cut down the language of the section
options.explanation: Illustrations explain the provision — where they cannot be reconciled with it, the operative words of the section govern.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Bare Act · Means and includes
questions.stem: A definitions clause says: "'goods' means every kind of movable property" and "'document' includes an electronic record". It follows that:

readLink.label: Read: How to read a bare Act →

options.text: Both definitions are exhaustive, the verb used making no difference
options.explanation: The verb is precisely what makes the difference — 'means' closes the definition, 'includes' opens it.

options.text: The definition of 'goods' is exhaustive, while 'document' bears its ordinary meaning enlarged to cover an electronic record
options.explanation: 'Means' confines the term to what is stated; 'includes' adds to the ordinary meaning rather than replacing it.

options.text: The definition of 'document' is exhaustive, so only an electronic record is a document
options.explanation: This reads an inclusive definition as a closed list — the classic error, and it produces an absurd result here.

options.text: Neither definition applies where the context otherwise requires, so both may be ignored at will
options.explanation: The 'unless the context otherwise requires' opening is a narrow safety valve, not a licence to disregard a definition.

questions.stem: Section 41 of an Act opens: 'Notwithstanding anything contained in section 30 …'. Section 30 says records may be destroyed after eight years; section 41 says records of a company in liquidation must be preserved until the liquidation concludes. For such a company:

readLink.label: Read: How to read a bare Act →

options.text: Section 30 prevails, being the earlier and more general provision
options.explanation: The non-obstante opening exists precisely to displace section 30; earlier numbering gives it no priority.

options.text: The two operate together, so records may be destroyed after eight years or at the end of the liquidation, whichever is earlier
options.explanation: There is no 'whichever is earlier' choice — the overriding provision replaces the general rule for the case it covers.

options.text: Section 41 overrides section 30, so the records must be preserved until the liquidation concludes
options.explanation: 'Notwithstanding anything contained in section 30' makes section 41 prevail wherever the two collide.

options.text: Section 41 is void, since a section cannot override another section of the same Act
options.explanation: A statute may certainly rank its own provisions; that is what a non-obstante clause does.

questions.stem: Enumerate the sources of law in India and explain the order of authority among them. Illustrate your answer with the position where a rule made under an Act conflicts with a section of that Act. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Six sources: the Constitution; legislation (Acts of Parliament and State Legislatures); subordinate or delegated legislation (rules, regulations, orders, bye-laws, notifications); judicial precedent; customs and usage; personal laws
The Constitution is supreme — every other source must conform to it, and a law inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of the inconsistency
Order of strength: Constitution, then statute, then delegated legislation, then an executive circular (which is administrative and lowest of all)

Precedent stands alongside rather than above: a judgment interprets the Constitution or a statute and does not override it; the legislature may amend the provision interpreted (Art. 141 binds courts, not Parliament)
Application: a rule inconsistent with its parent section is ultra vires and void to that extent; the section prevails, and a court may so hold without waiting for Parliament

questions.stem: Describe the stages through which a Bill passes before it becomes an Act of Parliament, and distinguish clearly between the assent of the President and the commencement of an Act. What is an Ordinance and how long does it last? (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Introduction in either House (a Money Bill only in the Lok Sabha), followed by the first reading — introduction and publication in the Gazette, with no debate on merits

Second reading — general discussion, often a reference to a Select or Standing Committee, then clause-by-clause consideration and amendments; third reading — the Bill is voted on as a whole; the other House then repeats the process, a deadlock on an ordinary Bill being resolvable in a joint sitting

Assent of the President, who may assent, withhold assent, or return an ordinary Bill once for reconsideration; on assent and publication in the Official Gazette the Bill becomes an Act with a number and year

Commencement is distinct from assent: an Act comes into force on the date it states or on a date notified by the Government, and different sections may be notified on different dates (the Companies Act 2013 is the standard example)

Ordinance: promulgated by the President when Parliament is not in session and immediate action is needed; it has the same force as an Act but must be laid before the legislature and ceases to operate six weeks after reassembly unless approved earlier

questions.stem: What is delegated legislation? Distinguish between rules, regulations, notifications and circulars, and state the limits within which delegated legislation must operate. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Meaning: the legislature lays down the policy and framework in the Act and authorises the executive to make detailed provisions; that subordinate law-making is delegated legislation
Rules — made by the Central or a State Government under a rule-making section of the parent Act (e.g. the Companies (Incorporation) Rules 2014 under s. 469 of the Companies Act 2013)

Regulations — made by a statutory regulator under its own Act (SEBI regulations, RBI directions); notifications — issued by Government in the Official Gazette, e.g. to bring sections into force, prescribe limits or grant exemptions
Circulars and clarifications — administrative instructions of a department or regulator; they guide officers and the public but cannot create a liability, take away a right, or contradict the statute

Limits: it must be intra vires the parent Act; where a rule conflicts with the section, the section prevails; and parent Acts commonly require rules to be laid before Parliament, which may modify or annul them
skeleton.citation: Doctrine of ultra vires; laying requirement

questions.stem: Explain the doctrine of stare decisis. Distinguish ratio decidendi from obiter dicta, and state which courts are bound by whose decisions in India. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Stare decisis — 'to stand by things decided': a point once decided is followed in later cases, so that like cases are decided alike and the law remains certain and predictable

Ratio decidendi — the legal principle on which the decision rests, applied to the material facts; this alone binds. Obiter dicta — observations made in passing, not necessary to the decision; persuasive only

The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts and tribunals within the territory of India; the Supreme Court is not bound by its own earlier decisions and may reconsider them, ordinarily through a larger Bench

A High Court binds all courts and tribunals within its own territorial jurisdiction and is only persuasive elsewhere; a single judge is bound by a Division or Full Bench of the same High Court; foreign judgments are persuasive only
A precedent may be distinguished (material facts differ), overruled (a higher court or larger Bench holds it wrong in law) or reversed (the same case decided the other way on appeal)

questions.stem: Distinguish between civil and criminal proceedings with reference to the purpose, the parties, the initiating document, the standard of proof and the outcome. Can the same set of facts give rise to both? (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Purpose: a civil proceeding enforces a right and compensates a loss; a criminal proceeding punishes a wrong against society, prosecuted in the name of the State
skeleton.citation: Nature of civil and criminal proceedings

skeleton.point: Parties and initiating document: plaintiff v defendant, begun by a plaint (suit) under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908; prosecution/State v accused, begun by prosecution or a private complaint under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023

Standard and burden of proof: civil — preponderance of probabilities, the burden lying on the plaintiff who asserts; criminal — beyond reasonable doubt, the burden on the prosecution, the accused being presumed innocent

Outcome: a decree — damages, injunction, specific performance, possession; against conviction or acquittal — fine or imprisonment. Civil suits may generally be compromised or withdrawn; criminal cases only where the offence is compoundable

Yes: the same facts may give rise to both, as with a dishonoured cheque (a civil suit for the money and a complaint under s. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881); the proceedings are independent and neither concludes the other

questions.stem: Explain the function of a proviso, an explanation and an illustration in a statute. Distinguish a definition that uses 'means' from one that uses 'includes', and state the effect of a non-obstante clause. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Structure: an Act contains a short title, long title and preamble, an extent and commencement section, definitions, substantive sections (divided into sub-sections, clauses and sub-clauses) and Schedules, which form part of the Act
Proviso — introduced by 'Provided that'; it carves an exception out of the provision to which it is attached, and only that provision, and is construed strictly
Explanation — it clarifies or extends the meaning of the main provision and may bring a case within the section; it cannot be read against the provision it explains
Illustration — a worked example supplied by the legislature; it aids understanding but cannot control or cut down the language of the section, which prevails on any irreconcilable conflict

'Means' makes a definition exhaustive; 'includes' makes it extensive, adding to the ordinary meaning so that the list is illustrative; 'means and includes' is exhaustive but expressly enlarged. Definitions ordinarily apply 'unless the context otherwise requires'

A non-obstante clause ('Notwithstanding anything contained in …') makes the provision override whatever it names, while 'subject to …' subordinates it; and 'shall' is ordinarily mandatory while 'may' is enabling or discretionary

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Jurisdiction and the court hierarchy · Case: routing a dispute
questions.case: Gokul Packaging, a proprietorship in Belgaum district, supplied corrugated cartons to Nandini Foods Private Limited, whose registered office and only factory are in the same district. Gokul has been unpaid for eleven months and claims ₹28,00,000 as the price of goods, plus ₹2,40,000 of interest claimed as part of the sum due. In that State a Civil Judge (Junior Division) may try suits valued up to ₹15,00,000; above that and up to ₹2,00,00,000 the Senior Civil Judge is competent; beyond ₹2,00,00,000 the District Judge. Gokul also alleges that Nandini's director induced the last two deliveries knowing the company could not pay, and separately Nandini's minority shareholders have moved the National Company Law Tribunal against the same director for oppression and mismanagement. All facts are as on 28 February 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Jurisdiction — three questions before you file →

questions.stem: The recovery claim by Gokul Packaging is properly characterised as:

options.text: A criminal complaint, because non-payment of a lawful debt is an offence
options.explanation: Non-payment of a debt is not by itself an offence; this sends a civil money claim into a criminal court.

options.text: A petition before the NCLT, the defendant being a company
options.explanation: The identity of the defendant does not decide the forum; the NCLT's jurisdiction covers company-law matters, not an ordinary trade debt.

options.text: A civil suit, the relief sought being money due under a contract of sale
options.explanation: The right asserted is contractual and the remedy is a decree for money, so the claim belongs on the civil side.

options.text: An arbitration reference, commercial disputes being arbitrable by default
options.explanation: Arbitration requires an agreement between the parties; there is no default reference merely because the dispute is commercial.

questions.stem: Applying the pecuniary limits stated, the suit must be filed before:

options.text: The Civil Judge (Junior Division), the limits being indicative only
options.explanation: Pecuniary limits are binding; a plaint above a court's competence is returned for presentation to the proper court.

options.text: The District Judge, ₹30,40,000 being a substantial commercial claim
options.explanation: Size in the colloquial sense is irrelevant; the District Judge's competence begins above ₹2,00,00,000.

options.text: The National Company Law Tribunal, since the defendant is a company
options.explanation: This confuses the character of the defendant with subject-matter jurisdiction; a trade-debt suit is not a company-law matter.

options.text: The Senior Civil Judge, the suit being valued at ₹30,40,000
options.explanation: ₹28,00,000 + ₹2,40,000 = ₹30,40,000, which exceeds the Junior Division's ₹15,00,000 ceiling and is within the Senior Civil Judge's ₹2,00,00,000 limit.

questions.stem: The shareholders' oppression and mismanagement petition is before the NCLT and is decided against them. Their appeal, and any further challenge on a question of law, lie respectively to:

options.text: The NCLAT, and thereafter the Supreme Court
options.explanation: An appeal from the NCLT lies to the NCLAT, and from an NCLAT order to the Supreme Court on a question of law.

options.text: The High Court, and thereafter the Supreme Court
options.explanation: This inserts the High Court into a route the Companies Act does not use for NCLT matters.

options.text: The District Judge, and thereafter the High Court
options.explanation: The civil hierarchy has no role here — the statute has assigned the subject to the tribunal and barred the civil court.

options.text: The Central Government, and thereafter the NCLAT
options.explanation: The executive does not sit in appeal over a tribunal's judicial order, and the NCLAT is not an appellate body over the Government.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Reading a bare Act · Case: a section with a proviso and an explanation
questions.case:
A (fictional) State enactment provides:

"14. Registration of dealers. (1) Every dealer whose turnover in a financial year exceeds ₹20,00,000 shall apply for registration within thirty days of exceeding that turnover:

Provided that a dealer dealing exclusively in exempted goods shall not be required to apply under this sub-section.

Explanation.— For the purposes of this section, 'turnover' includes the value of goods supplied to a branch of the dealer situated outside the State.

Illustration.— A dealer whose turnover is ₹19,00,000 need not apply."

Kavya is a dealer in that State. In the financial year her sales of taxable goods were ₹17,00,000 and she also despatched goods worth ₹4,00,000 to her own branch in a neighbouring State. She also sells a small quantity of exempted goods. A departmental circular issued last year states that a dealer's turnover 'shall be computed without regard to branch despatches'. All facts are as on 28 February 2026.

readLink.label: Read: How to read a bare Act →

questions.stem: Kavya's turnover for the purposes of section 14, and the effect on her liability to apply, are:

options.text: ₹17,00,000 — below the limit, branch despatches being transfers rather than sales
options.explanation: This ignores the Explanation, which expressly brings branch supplies outside the State into 'turnover' for this section.

options.text: ₹21,00,000 — above the limit, so she must apply within thirty days of crossing ₹20,00,000
options.explanation: ₹17,00,000 + ₹4,00,000 = ₹21,00,000; the Explanation extends the meaning of turnover, and the duty in sub-section (1) is triggered.

options.text: ₹21,00,000 — but no duty arises, an Explanation being unable to create a liability
options.explanation: The duty is created by sub-section (1); the Explanation only fixes the meaning of a word used in it, which is exactly what an Explanation may do.

options.text: ₹19,00,000 — the figure the Illustration treats as below the limit
options.explanation: An illustration is an example, not a rule of computation; borrowing its figure in place of the facts is a serious misreading.

questions.stem: Kavya relies on the proviso, saying she deals in exempted goods. The proviso:
questions.sourceRef: Function of a proviso; strict construction

options.text: Does not help her, since it exempts only a dealer dealing exclusively in exempted goods and she also deals in taxable goods
options.explanation: A proviso is an exception and is read strictly; the word 'exclusively' confines it to dealers who handle nothing else.

options.text: Helps her in proportion to her exempted turnover, so only the taxable part need be registered
options.explanation: The proviso admits of no apportionment — it either applies to the dealer or it does not.

options.text: Helps her, a proviso being read liberally in favour of the assessee
options.explanation: Exceptions are construed strictly, not liberally; this inverts the rule of construction.

options.text: Cannot apply at all, because a proviso cannot exempt anyone from the main provision
options.explanation: Exempting a described case from the main provision is precisely what a proviso does; the point here is that Kavya is not that case.

questions.stem: Kavya then relies on the departmental circular saying turnover is computed without regard to branch despatches. The circular:
questions.sourceRef: Status of executive circulars; hierarchy of sources

options.text: Prevails, being the department's own understanding of the section it administers
options.explanation: Administrative understanding is not a source of law; the enacted words, including the Explanation, govern.

options.text: Prevails, because it is more recent than the Act
options.explanation: Recency gives an administrative instruction no priority over a statute; only an amending Act could change the Explanation.

options.text: Prevails to the extent it is beneficial to the dealer, circulars being binding when favourable
options.explanation: A favourable circular may bind departmental officers administratively, but it cannot displace the statutory meaning in a dispute about liability.

options.text: Cannot override the Explanation, a circular being administrative and unable to contradict the statute
options.explanation: A circular sits at the bottom of the hierarchy — it cannot cut down or contradict what the section and its Explanation provide.
